l: the crafty (the wise in their own craftiness), The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: God frustrates the plans of the crafty so their hands cannot carry out their enterprise. He takes the wise in their own craftiness, and the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong. They meet darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night.

l: the poor and needy, The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: The needy are saved by God from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty. As a result the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.

l: the listener (the one addressed), The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: The listener is asked whether anyone will answer him and to which of the holy ones he will turn. He is told not to despise the chastening of the Almighty and is promised deliverance in six troubles and in seven, redemption in famine and war, and hiding from the scourge of the tongue. He is also promised peace with the animals, a peaceful tent, great offspring, and a grave reached in full age, and is urged to hear and know it for his good.

l: trouble and affliction, The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: Affliction does not come out of the dust, nor does trouble spring out of the ground. Man is born to trouble as sparks fly upward. God delivers from it, and in seven troubles no evil will touch the one he delivers.

l: God's correction and deliverance, The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: The man whom God corrects is called happy, and the chastening of the Almighty is not to be despised because God wounds and binds up, injures and makes whole. Deliverance is promised in six troubles and seven, redeeming from death in famine and from the sword in war. It brings fearlessness toward destruction, peace with the animals of the field, a secure tent and fold, great offspring, and a full age.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 6
s: In Chapter 6, Job answers his friends, saying his anguish is heavier than the sand of the seas and that this is why his words have been rash. He describes the arrows and terrors of the Almighty as being within him, and he longs for God to crush him and cut him off, taking consolation that he has not denied the words of the Holy One. He rebukes his friends for lacking kindness, comparing his brothers to brooks that vanish in the dry season and leave caravans from Tema and Sheba confounded. He challenges the friends to teach him his error, accuses them of reproving the words of a desperate man and of treating a friend as merchandise, and insists that his cause is righteous and that there is no injustice on his tongue.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 6
s: Job answers his friends, saying his anguish outweighs the sand of the seas and excusing his rash words on that ground. He wishes God would crush him and cut him off, yet takes consolation that he has not denied the words of the Holy One. He asks to be shown his error, accuses his brothers of deceit, and insists his cause is righteous and his tongue free of injustice.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 6
s: God is described by Job as the Almighty whose arrows are within him, whose poison his spirit drinks, and whose terrors are set in array against him. Job wishes that God would be pleased to crush him and let loose his hand to cut him off. Job also calls God the Holy One, whose words he says he has not denied.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 6
s: Job says that a faint man should be shown kindness by his friend, and he accuses his brothers of dealing deceitfully like brooks that vanish. He says they are now nothing, seeing a terror and being afraid, and that their reproof reproves nothing. He charges that they would cast lots for the fatherless and make merchandise of a friend, and he asks them to look at him, return, and let there be no injustice.

l: brooks (Job's brothers' comparison), The Book of Job, Chapter 6
s: Job compares his brothers' deceitful dealing to brooks that are dark with ice and snow but vanish in the dry season and are consumed in the heat. Caravans that travel beside them turn away, go up into the waste, and perish. The caravans of Tema and the companies of Sheba looked and waited for them, and were distressed and confounded because they had been confident.

l: Job's anguish and calamity, The Book of Job, Chapter 6
s: Job wishes his anguish were weighed and his calamity laid in the balances, saying it would be heavier than the sand of the seas. He gives it as the reason his words have been rash. He links it to the arrows, poison, and terrors of God within and against him, and says it leaves him without strength, help, or wisdom.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 7
s: In Chapter 7 the speaker, Job, reflects on the hardship and brevity of human life, comparing it to the toil of a hired hand and describing his own months of misery, sleepless nights, and afflicted skin covered with worms and dust. He says his days pass swiftly and without hope, and that death, going down to Sheol, is final, with no return to his house. Vowing not to keep silent, he complains in the bitterness of his soul and addresses God directly. He asks whether he is a sea or sea monster that God must guard him, and accuses God of terrifying him with dreams and visions when he seeks rest. He says he loathes his life, asks why God magnifies and tests man so closely, and asks why God does not pardon his disobedience, since soon he will lie in the dust and God will seek him but he will not be.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 7
s: Job describes his suffering as months of misery and wearisome nights, with flesh clothed in worms and dust and skin that closes and breaks out afresh. He vows not to keep silent and complains to God in the bitterness of his soul, saying he loathes his life and would choose strangling and death. He asks why God watches and burdens him, and why God does not pardon his disobedience, noting that he will soon lie in the dust and be no more.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 7
s: God is addressed by Job as the 'watcher of men' who places a guard over him, scares him with dreams and terrifies him with visions. Job accuses God of magnifying man, visiting him every morning, testing him every moment, and not looking away from him or leaving him alone. Job asks God to remember that his life is a breath and to pardon his iniquity, and says God will one day seek him but he will not be.

l: human life (its brevity and misery), The Book of Job, Chapter 7
s: Human life is portrayed as forced labor on earth, with days like those of a hired hand who longs for the shadow and for his wages. Job says his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and spent without hope, and that life is a breath. He says his eye will no more see good.

l: death, The Book of Job, Chapter 7
s: Death is described as final: like a cloud that is consumed and vanishes, he who goes down to Sheol will come up no more. The dead return no more to their houses and their place knows them no more. Job says the eye that sees him will see him no more, and that he will soon lie down in the dust. He says he would choose death over his bones and suffering.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 8
s: Bildad the Shuhite responds to the one he addresses, rebuking him for speaking like a mighty wind and insisting that God does not pervert justice. He suggests that the addressee's children died because of their own sin, and urges him to seek God and be pure and upright so that God would restore him and make his latter end greater. Bildad appeals to the wisdom of past generations and uses images of papyrus and rushes withering without water, and a spider's web, to show that the hope of those who forget God perishes. He closes by asserting that God will not cast away a blameless man or uphold evildoers, and that the addressee will again have laughter while his haters are clothed with shame and the tent of the wicked is no more.

l: Bildad the Shuhite, The Book of Job, Chapter 8
s: Bildad the Shuhite answers, rebuking the addressee's words as a mighty wind and defending God's justice. He claims that the addressee's children sinned and were delivered into their disobedience, urges seeking God, and appeals to the teaching of past generations, admitting that he and his companions are but of yesterday and know nothing.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 8
s: God is described by Bildad as one who does not pervert justice or righteousness, and who delivered the addressee's children into the hand of their disobedience. Bildad says God would awaken for a pure and upright person, will not cast away a blameless man, will not uphold evildoers, and will fill the addressee's mouth with laughter and his lips with shouting.

l: Job (the addressee of Bildad), The Book of Job, Chapter 8
s: Job is addressed by Bildad, who rebukes his speech as a mighty wind and suggests his children sinned against God. He is urged to seek God and supplicate the Almighty, and is told that if he were pure and upright, God would restore him so that his small beginning would be followed by great increase. Bildad promises that God will fill his mouth with laughter and that those who hate him will be clothed with shame.

l: godless man, The Book of Job, Chapter 8
s: The godless man is depicted as one who forgets God, whose hope perishes and whose confidence and trust are like a spider's web. He leans on his house but it does not stand, and though he flourishes green before the sun, if he is destroyed from his place it denies him, and others spring up from the earth in his stead.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Job, Chapter 8
s: Bildad asks rhetorically whether God perverts justice or the Almighty perverts righteousness, implying that he does not. He presents them as the basis for his claims that sin brings destruction, that the blameless are not cast away, and that evildoers are not upheld.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 9
s: In Chapter 9, Job answers a previous speaker by asking how a man can be just with God. He describes God's overwhelming power over mountains, earth, sun, stars, heavens and sea, and says God passes by him unseen and cannot be challenged. Job says he could not argue his case or trust that God would hear him, since God breaks him with a storm and multiplies his wounds without cause. He claims to be blameless, yet says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike and lets the earth fall into the hands of the wicked. He laments that his days are fleeing, that no washing can make him clean before God, and that there is no umpire between them, and he wishes God's rod and terror removed so he could speak without fear.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 9
s: Job responds by asking how man can be just with God, and says he could not answer God once in a thousand times. He insists he is blameless yet believes his own mouth would condemn him, and that God would not hold him innocent. He says his days pass swifter than a runner, that he cannot forget his complaint or cheer up, and that washing himself with snow would not help. He longs for an umpire between himself and God, and wishes God's rod and terror removed so he could speak without fear.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 9
s: God is described as wise in heart and mighty in strength, removing mountains, shaking the earth, commanding the sun, sealing up the stars, stretching out the heavens and treading on the waves. He makes the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades and the rooms of the south, and does marvelous things past finding out. Job says God passes by unseen, snatches away with no one able to hinder him, and does not withdraw his anger, for the helpers of Rahab stoop under him. Job accuses him of breaking him with a storm, multiplying his wounds without cause, destroying the blameless and the wicked alike, and mocking the trial of the innocent. Job also says God is not a man and has no umpire between himself and Job.

l: justice of man before God, The Book of Job, Chapter 9
s: Job opens by asking how man can be just with God, and concludes it is hopeless to contend with him. A person could not answer God once in a thousand times, and even if righteous or blameless, Job says his own mouth would condemn him and prove him perverse. Job argues that if the matter is one of strength, God is mighty, and if of justice, no one can summon him. He says there is no umpire to lay a hand on both parties, and that even washing with snow and lye would leave him plunged into the ditch.

l: Job's suffering, The Book of Job, Chapter 9
s: Job describes his suffering as being broken with a storm, having wounds multiplied without cause, being unable to catch his breath, and being filled with bitterness. He says his days flee swiftly like runners, swift ships and a swooping eagle, and see no good. He fears all his sorrows, says he despises his life, and sees no point in laboring in vain. He holds that the suffering falls alike on the blameless and the wicked, and wishes God's rod and terror taken from him.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 10
s: In Chapter 10, the speaker, weary of his life, resolves to voice his bitter complaint to God and asks not to be condemned. He questions whether God, who does not see as mortals do, needs to hunt for his sin when God knows he is not wicked. He recalls that God's hands formed him like clay, knit him with skin, flesh, bones and sinews, and granted him life and loving kindness, yet God now seems to destroy him. He says that whether he is wicked or righteous he is filled with disgrace, and that God hunts him like a lion. He wishes he had died at birth, and asks God to leave him alone for a little comfort before he goes to the dark land of the shadow of death.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 10
s: God is addressed by the speaker, who asks why he contends with him, and accuses him of oppressing the work of his hands and of searching after his sin though he knows he is not wicked. God is said to have fashioned the speaker, granted him life and loving kindness, and preserved his spirit, yet is also described as hunting him like a lion and renewing witnesses and indignation against him. The speaker asks God whether he has eyes of flesh and whether his days are like those of mortals.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 10
s: Job, weary of his life, gives free course to his complaint and speaks in bitterness of soul to God. He pleads not to be condemned, maintains that God knows he is not wicked, and says that even if righteous he cannot lift his head for disgrace. He wishes he had died at birth and asks to be left alone for a little comfort before he dies.

l: Job's affliction, The Book of Job, Chapter 10
s: Job says he is conscious of his affliction and filled with disgrace. He describes it as God hunting him like a lion, renewing witnesses against him, and increasing indignation, so that changes and warfare are with him. He says it comes whether he sins or is righteous.

l: Job's creation and formation, The Book of Job, Chapter 10
s: Job recalls that God's hands framed and fashioned him altogether like clay, poured him out like milk and curdled him like cheese. He says God clothed him with skin and flesh and knit him together with bones and sinews, and granted him life and loving kindness. He asks why God, having made him, would destroy him and return him to dust, and wishes he had been carried from the womb to the grave.

l: land of darkness (Sheol), The Book of Job, Chapter 10
s: Job describes it as the land of darkness and the shadow of death, from which one does not return. He portrays it as dark as midnight, without order, and with light like midnight. He says his few days are running out before he goes there.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 11
s: Zophar, the Naamathite, answers the previous speaker in Chapter 11, accusing him of being full of talk, mocking, and claiming his doctrine is pure and that he is clean in God's eyes. Zophar wishes God would speak against him and says God exacts less than his iniquity deserves. He describes the mystery of God as higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, and broader than the sea, so that no one can oppose God. He then urges the addressee to set his heart aright, stretch out his hands to God, and put away iniquity, promising security, clarity, and rest. He closes by saying the eyes of the wicked will fail and their hope will be the giving up of the spirit.

l: Zophar the Naamathite, The Book of Job, Chapter 11
s: Zophar answers by rebuking the addressee's many words and mockery, and quotes him as claiming a pure doctrine and cleanness before God. He wishes God would speak against the addressee, declares God's mystery unfathomable, and urges repentance with promises of restored security. He ends by warning that the wicked will have no escape.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 11
s: God is described by Zophar as one who could speak and open his lips against the addressee, and who exacts less than the addressee's iniquity deserves. He knows false men and sees iniquity, and when he passes by, confines, or convenes a court, no one can oppose him. Zophar urges the addressee to stretch out his hands toward God.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job, Chapter 11
s: The addressee is accused by Zophar of being a man full of talk, of boasting and mocking, and of claiming 'My doctrine is pure. I am clean in your eyes.' Zophar says he deserves more punishment than God exacts, and urges him to set his heart aright, stretch out his hands to God, and put away iniquity. If he does, Zophar promises he will lift his face without spot, forget his misery, be secure, rest in safety, and be courted by many.

l: the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 11
s: Zophar says the eyes of the wicked will fail and they will have no way to flee. Their hope will be the giving up of the spirit.

l: mystery of God, The Book of Job, Chapter 11
s: Zophar asks whether the addressee can fathom the mystery of God or probe the limits of the Almighty. He describes it as high as heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth, and broader than the sea, beyond what a person can do or know.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: In Chapter 12, Job answers his friends with sarcasm, saying they think wisdom will die with them while he has understanding equal to theirs. He complains that he, a just and blameless man who called on God and was answered, has become a joke to his neighbor, while robbers' tents prosper and those who provoke God are secure. He tells them to ask the animals, birds, earth, and fish, which all know that the LORD's hand has done this and that every living thing's life and breath is in his hand. Job then declares that wisdom, might, counsel, and understanding belong to God, and describes how God breaks down what cannot be rebuilt, withholds and sends the waters, and strips counselors, judges, kings, priests, and princes of their power. He adds that God raises and destroys nations and takes understanding from the chiefs of the earth so that they grope in the dark and stagger like drunkards.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: Job answers his friends sarcastically, claiming he has understanding equal to theirs and is not inferior. He laments that though he is just and blameless and called on God, who answered him, he has become a joke to his neighbor. He then affirms that wisdom, might, and control over rulers and nations belong to God.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: God is described as the one in whose hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind. With him are wisdom, might, counsel, and understanding. He breaks down, imprisons, withholds and sends waters, strips counselors, judges, kings, priests, and princes, uncovers deep things, and increases and destroys nations. Job also says he answered Job when Job called on him.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: Job addresses his friends as 'the people' with whom wisdom will die, mocking their claim to wisdom. He insists he is not inferior to them and that everyone knows the things they have said. He tells them to learn from the animals, birds, earth, and fish.

l: wisdom and understanding, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: Job says that wisdom is with the aged and understanding with length of days, but that wisdom and might truly are with God, who also has counsel and understanding. God takes understanding away from elders, trusted speakers, and the chiefs of the people of the earth, leaving them wandering without a way. Job claims to have understanding as well as his friends.

l: robbers, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: Job observes that the tents of robbers prosper. Those who provoke God are secure, carrying their god in their hands. He cites this as part of the unfairness he sees, alongside the contempt shown to the just and blameless.

l: God's sovereign power over the world, The Book of Job, Chapter 12
s: Job describes God's power as extending over nature and human affairs: he breaks down what cannot be rebuilt, imprisons without release, withholds the waters so they dry up, and sends them to overturn the earth. He leads away counselors, judges, priests, and the mighty, loosens kings' bonds, pours contempt on princes, and enlarges and destroys nations. He makes leaders grope in the dark and stagger like drunkards.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 13
s: The speaker, who is in a dispute with God, tells his friends that he knows as much as they do and is not inferior to them. He calls them forgers of lies and worthless physicians, and accuses them of speaking deceitfully and showing partiality on God's behalf, warning that God will reprove them. He resolves to speak and present his case to God even at the risk of his life, saying that he has set his cause in order and knows he is righteous. He then asks God to withdraw his hand and terror from him, and to either call or answer him, and he demands to know his iniquities and sins. He closes by lamenting that God hides his face, treats him as an enemy, writes bitter things against him, confines his feet, and leaves him decaying like a rotten thing or a moth-eaten garment.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 13
s: Job declares that he has seen and understood all that his friends know and is not inferior to them. He says he wants to reason with God, will maintain his ways even though he expects God to kill him, and believes he is righteous. He asks God to withdraw his hand and terror, to tell him his sins, and laments that he is treated as an enemy and is decaying like a rotten thing.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 13
s: God is the one whom the speaker desires to reason with, and he is said to be able to search out and reprove those who show him secret partiality. The speaker describes God's majesty and dread as fearful, and accuses him of hiding his face, treating the speaker as an enemy, writing bitter things against him, putting his feet in the stocks and marking all his paths. The speaker asks him to call or answer and to make known his sins.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 13
s: Job's friends are called forgers of lies and physicians of no value, and he wishes they would be completely silent so that they would be wise. He accuses them of speaking unrighteously and deceitfully for God and showing partiality, warns that God will reprove them and make them afraid, and calls their sayings proverbs of ashes and their defenses defenses of clay.

l: Job's complaint, The Book of Job, Chapter 13
s: Job says he has set his cause in order and knows he is righteous, and he asks who will contend with him, since he would then be silent and give up the spirit. He wants to plead it before God and to be told what his iniquities and sins are, and he intends to maintain his ways before God even though he expects to be killed.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 14
s: In Chapter 14 the speaker laments the brevity and frailty of human life, describing man as born of woman, short-lived, full of trouble, and fleeting like a flower or shadow. He asks God why He brings such a creature into judgment, noting that man's days and bounds are fixed by God. The speaker contrasts man with a tree, which can sprout again after being cut down, whereas man dies and does not rise. He wishes God would hide him in Sheol until His wrath passed and then remember him, and wonders whether a dead man might live again. He ends by saying God counts his steps and seals up his sin, destroys man's hope like water wearing away stones, and leaves the dead ignorant of their sons while the flesh feels pain and the soul mourns.

l: man, The Book of Job, Chapter 14
s: Man is described as born of a woman, of few days, full of trouble, and like a flower cut down or a shadow that does not last. His days and months are determined by God, who has set bounds he cannot pass. When he dies he lies down and does not rise, and in death he does not know whether his sons are honored or brought low.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 14
s: God is addressed as the one who opens his eyes on man, brings him into judgment, and appoints the number of his months and his bounds. The speaker accuses Him of counting his steps, sealing up his sin in a bag, and forever prevailing against man, destroying his hope. The speaker also imagines God hiding him in Sheol until His wrath is past, then remembering him and desiring the work of His hands.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 14
s: The speaker laments human frailty and asks God to look away from man so he may rest like a hireling finishing his day. He wishes to be hidden in Sheol until God's wrath passes, says he would wait all the days of his warfare for release, and imagines answering God's call. He feels watched for his sin and ends in pain, with his soul mourning within him.

l: death and the hope of afterlife, The Book of Job, Chapter 14
s: Death is portrayed as final: man dies, gives up the spirit, and lies down and does not rise until the heavens are no more, like waters failing from the sea. The speaker asks whether a man who dies will live again and says he would wait for his release if so, but he offers no confirmation. The text compares God's destruction of man's hope to water wearing stones and washing away dust.

l: tree, The Book of Job, Chapter 14
s: The tree is presented as having hope that man lacks: if cut down it will sprout again, and its tender branch will not cease. Even when its root grows old in the earth and its stock dies in the ground, the scent of water makes it bud and put out boughs like a plant.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 15
s: Eliphaz the Temanite answers his addressee, rebuking him for speaking empty, unprofitable words that undermine fear and devotion before God. He asks whether the addressee is the first man born, holds God's secret counsel, or knows more than the aged and gray-headed among them, and he says the addressee's own mouth condemns him. He argues that no man is clean or righteous before God, whose holy ones and heavens are not pure in his sight. Eliphaz then declares what he has seen and what wise men received from their fathers: the wicked man suffers terror and pain all his days, is pursued by the sword and darkness, and loses his wealth because he defied the Almighty. He closes by saying the godless company will be barren, their tents consumed by fire, as they conceive mischief and produce iniquity.

l: Eliphaz the Temanite, The Book of Job, Chapter 15
s: Eliphaz the Temanite answers by rebuking the addressee as a speaker of vain knowledge who turns his spirit against God. He appeals to the authority of the aged and of wise men's tradition, and declares what he has seen about the wicked: that they suffer terror, loss, and destruction.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job, Chapter 15
s: Job, the one Eliphaz addresses, is accused of speaking vain and unprofitable words, doing away with fear, and hindering devotion before God. Eliphaz says his own mouth and lips condemn him, questions whether he is the first man born or holds God's counsel, and charges that his heart carries him away so that he lets words against God leave his mouth.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 15
s: God is described as having secret counsel and consolations that Eliphaz says are gentle toward the addressee. He is said to put no trust in his holy ones, to regard even the heavens as unclean, and to destroy the wicked by the breath of his mouth.

l: wicked man, The Book of Job, Chapter 15
s: The wicked man is portrayed as an oppressor who stretches out his hand against God, behaves proudly against the Almighty, and runs at him with a stiff neck. He is said to writhe in pain all his days, hear terrors, wander for bread, and see his wealth, branches, and fruit fail.

l: fate of the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 15
s: Eliphaz says the wicked live in torment all their years, with a destroyer coming even in prosperity, and that they will not escape darkness or the sword. Their riches will not last, their branch will wither before its time, and fire will consume the tents of the godless, whose trust in emptiness brings emptiness as reward.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 16
s: In Chapter 16, Job answers his friends, calling them miserable comforters and saying he could speak as they do if their places were reversed, though he would strengthen rather than accuse them. He describes his grief as unrelieved whether he speaks or stays silent, and he says God has worn him out, shriveled him, and made his company desolate. Job portrays God as an adversary who tears, breaks, and targets him with archers, and who hands him over to the wicked. He says he wears sackcloth and weeps, yet insists there is no violence in his hands and his prayer is pure. He appeals to the earth not to cover his blood, claims a witness in heaven who vouches for him, and weeps to God, asking that God maintain his right, since he will soon go the way of no return.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 16
s: Job answers his friends, calling them miserable comforters and saying he could speak as they do, but would instead strengthen them. He says God has worn him out and broken him, and he mourns in sackcloth with his horn in the dust. He maintains there is no violence in his hands and that his prayer is pure, and he declares that he has a witness in heaven who vouches for him. He pours out tears to God, asks that his right be maintained, and notes that he will soon go the way of no return.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 16
s: Job accuses God of wearing him out, making his company desolate, shriveling him, and tearing him in wrath. He says God delivers him to the ungodly, breaks him apart, sets him up as a target, and surrounds him with archers who do not spare him. Job also appeals to God with tears and asks that God maintain the right of a man with God, and he says his witness and the one who vouches for him is in heaven on high.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 16
s: Job's friends are called miserable comforters who have spoken many such things and vain words. Job says that if their places were reversed he could join words against them and shake his head at them, but he would rather strengthen and relieve them. He says they scoff at him.

l: Job's grief and suffering, The Book of Job, Chapter 16
s: Job's grief is not subsided whether he speaks or holds back. His body is shriveled and lean, his face is red with weeping, and deep darkness is on his eyelids. He describes being torn, gnashed at, struck on the cheek, broken apart, and pierced in the kidneys, with his bile poured on the ground, and he wears sackcloth sewn on his skin.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 17
s: In Chapter 17 the speaker declares his spirit consumed and his days extinct, with the grave ready for him, and says mockers surround him. He asks to be given a pledge, since no one will strike hands with him, and says that the one addressed has hidden his opponents' hearts from understanding. He describes being made a byword, spat upon, and dimmed in eye by sorrow, while upright men are astonished and the righteous hold to their way. He tells his opponents to come back, saying he will find no wise man among them. He ends by saying his days and plans are broken, and asks where his hope is if he makes Sheol his house, calling corruption his father and the worm his mother and sister, and whether his hope will go down to Sheol's gates and into the dust.

l: Sheol, The Book of Job, Chapter 17
s: Job speaks of looking for Sheol as his house and spreading his couch in the darkness. He asks whether his hope will go down with him to the gates of Sheol and descend together into the dust.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 18
s: In Chapter 18, Bildad the Shuhite answers by rebuking the person he addresses for hunting for words and treating his companions as unclean animals. He insists the earth will not be forsaken nor the rock moved for the angry listener. Most of the speech describes the fate of the wicked: his light and lamp are put out, his steps shortened, and he is caught in nets, snares, traps, and a hidden noose. Terrors chase him, death devours his body, and he is rooted out of his tent and brought to the king of terrors. His roots dry up, his memory perishes, he leaves no son or grandson, and later generations are astonished at his day, as such are the dwellings of those who do not know God.

l: Bildad the Shuhite, The Book of Job, Chapter 18
s: Bildad the Shuhite answers by asking how long his listener will hunt for words and by protesting that he and his companions are counted as unclean animals. He then delivers a long description of the wicked man's ruin, ending with the claim that such is the dwelling of one who does not know God.

l: Job (the addressee of Bildad), The Book of Job, Chapter 18
s: Job is addressed by Bildad as one who hunts for words and who tears himself in his anger. Bildad complains that he and his companions are regarded as animals in Job's sight, and asks whether the earth will be forsaken or the rock removed for Job's sake.

l: the wicked (the wicked man), The Book of Job, Chapter 18
s: The wicked man is said to face a fall: his strength is shortened and famished, his own counsel casts him down, and terrors chase him. He is devoured by the firstborn of death, rooted out of his tent, and brought to the king of terrors. His memory perishes, he has no name in the street, he is driven from light into darkness and out of the world, and he leaves no son or grandson. Those who come after are astonished at his day.

l: light of the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 18
s: The light of the wicked is said to be put out, and the spark of his fire will not shine. The light becomes dark in his tent and his lamp above him is extinguished. He is later driven from light into darkness.

l: traps and snares (for the wicked), The Book of Job, Chapter 18
s: The wicked man is cast into a net by his own feet and wanders into its mesh. A snare takes him by the heel, a trap catches him, and a noose is hidden for him in the ground and on the path.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 19
s: In Chapter 19, Job answers his friends, accusing them of tormenting him with words and reproaching him repeatedly. He insists that God has wronged and besieged him, stripping his glory, breaking down his hope, and counting him as an adversary. He laments that his brothers, relatives, friends, servants, wife, and even young children have turned from him, and that he has barely escaped with his life. He pleads for pity from his friends and wishes his words were engraved in rock forever. He declares his confidence that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God in his flesh, and warns his friends to fear the sword of judgment.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 19
s: Job rebukes his friends for tormenting him and says that if he has erred, the error remains with himself. He laments that God has walled up his way, stripped his glory, and that his family, servants, and friends have all turned from him. He pleads for pity, wishes his words were engraved in rock, and declares that he knows his Redeemer lives and that he will see God in his flesh.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 19
s: God is described by Job as having subverted him, surrounded him with a net, walled up his path, set darkness in it, and kindled wrath against him as though he were an adversary. Job says God's hand has touched him, and that his troops besiege his tent. Job nonetheless expects to see God in his flesh, on his side and not as a stranger.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 19
s: Job's friends are accused of crushing him with words, reproaching him ten times, and shamelessly attacking him. Job asks them to have pity, asks why they persecute him as God does without being satisfied with his flesh, and warns them to fear the sword, since wrath brings its punishments and there is a judgment.

l: Redeemer (Job's Redeemer), The Book of Job, Chapter 19
s: Job declares that he knows his Redeemer lives and that in the end he will stand upon the earth. Job expects that after his skin is destroyed he will see God in his flesh with his own eyes, with the Redeemer on his side.

l: Job's suffering, The Book of Job, Chapter 19
s: Job's suffering includes the loss of his glory and crown, the uprooting of his hope, and estrangement from brothers, relatives, friends, servants, wife, and children. His breath is offensive to his wife, his bones cling to his skin and flesh, and he has escaped only by the skin of his teeth. He says he cries out of wrong but receives no justice.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 20
s: In Chapter 20, Zophar the Naamathite responds to the reproof he has heard by insisting that the triumph of the wicked is brief and the joy of the godless lasts only a moment. He describes how a wicked man, though he rises to the heavens, will perish like his own dung, vanish like a dream, and be forgotten by those who saw him. His ill-gotten riches, sweet in his mouth, turn to cobra venom; he must vomit them up, and he is not allowed to enjoy them because he oppressed and forsook the poor and seized houses. God casts his wrath on him, and he is struck by weapons, terrors, and unfanned fire, while heaven and earth testify against him. Zophar concludes that this is the portion and heritage God appoints for a wicked man.

l: Zophar the Naamathite, The Book of Job, Chapter 20
s: Zophar the Naamathite answers, speaking out of haste and saying he has heard a reproof that shames him. He argues from ancient knowledge that the wicked man's triumph is short, and closes by declaring that such ruin is the wicked man's portion from God.

l: wicked man (Zophar's subject), The Book of Job, Chapter 20
s: The wicked man is described as one whose height may reach the heavens yet who perishes forever and is not found, like a dream. He oppressed and forsook the poor, devoured all, and knew no quietness, so he cannot enjoy or keep his gains; his children seek the poor's favor, and he is struck down by God's wrath, with heaven and earth against him.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 20
s: God is portrayed as the one who casts the wicked man's swallowed riches out of his belly and who casts the fierceness of his wrath on him, raining it on him while he eats. Zophar says the wicked man's fate is his portion and the heritage appointed to him by God.

l: riches (the wicked man's wealth), The Book of Job, Chapter 20
s: The wicked man's riches are said to be swallowed down but then vomited up, as God casts them out of his belly. His hands give back his wealth, he restores what he labored for without enjoying it, and the increase of his house departs on the day of wrath, while darkness is laid up for his treasures.

l: downfall of the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 20
s: Zophar describes the downfall as sudden and certain: the triumph of the wicked is short, and distress overtakes him in the fullness of his sufficiency. It includes perishing like dung, vanishing like a dream, being struck by a bronze arrow, being consumed by unfanned fire, and having the heavens reveal his iniquity and the earth rise against him.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: In Chapter 21, Job answers his friends, asking them to listen to him and let that be their consolation before they resume mocking him. He challenges their claim that the wicked are punished in this life by asking why the wicked live long, grow powerful, see their children established, and enjoy safe houses, thriving livestock, music, and prosperity until they go down to Sheol. He notes that such people tell God to depart, yet Job says their prosperity is not in their own hand and he rejects their counsel. He argues that one man dies at ease and another in bitterness, yet both lie alike in the dust, and that the evil man is honored at his grave with no one repaying him. He ends by calling his friends' comfort nonsense and their answers falsehood.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: Job answers his friends, asking them to listen and to let that be their consolation, and says his complaint is not to man and that he is impatient. He argues that the wicked often prosper and die at ease, rejecting their counsel, and accuses his friends of plotting to wrong him. He concludes that their comfort is nonsense and their answers remain only falsehood.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: Job's friends are told to listen, be astonished, and lay their hands on their mouths, and Job expects them to mock him after he speaks. Job says he knows their thoughts and plans to wrong him, quotes their assertion about the house of the prince and the tent of the wicked, and tells them to ask wayfaring men. He declares their comfort nonsense and their answers falsehood.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: God is portrayed as one whom the wicked tell to depart because they do not want to know his ways, and whom they question as to what profit there is in serving him. Job notes that the rod of God is not upon the wicked's houses, and asks whether anyone can teach God knowledge, since he judges those who are high. Job also challenges the claim that God lays up a man's iniquity for his children, saying the man himself should be repaid.

l: the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: The wicked are described as living, growing old, and becoming mighty, with children established before their eyes, safe houses, and children who dance and sing. They tell God to depart and ask what profit there is in serving the Almighty. They go down to Sheol in an instant, are carried to the grave and watched over at the tomb, and no one declares their way to their face or repays them.

l: prosperity of the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: Job describes it as including long life, power, secure descendants, houses free of fear, livestock that breed and calve without fail, and music and rejoicing. He says it is not in the wicked's own hand, and that one may die in full strength, at ease, with pails full of milk. He uses it as evidence against his friends' claims.

l: divine retribution, The Book of Job, Chapter 21
s: Job disputes the friends' view that calamity regularly overtakes the wicked, asking how often their lamp is put out or they are like chaff before the wind. He rejects the idea that God stores up a man's iniquity for his children and says the offender himself should see his destruction and drink the Almighty's wrath. He observes that the fortunate and the embittered die alike and lie together in the dust, and that the evil man is reserved for a day of calamity and wrath.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: Eliphaz the Temanite answers the man he addresses, arguing that God gains nothing from human righteousness and that the man's suffering must come from great wickedness. He accuses him of taking pledges for nothing, stripping the naked, withholding water and bread, and sending widows away empty. He says snares, sudden fear, darkness and floods surround the man as a result. Eliphaz then describes God as high above the heavens and warns against following the old way of wicked men who were snatched away before their time. He closes by urging the man to acquaint himself with God, return to the Almighty, and put away unrighteousness, promising treasure, answered prayer, light on his ways, and deliverance through clean hands.

l: Eliphaz the Temanite, The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: Eliphaz the Temanite answers with a speech that accuses the man he addresses of great wickedness and endless iniquities. He lists specific wrongs, describes God's height and the fate of wicked men, and ends by urging return to the Almighty with promises of restoration.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: God is described as one who gains no profit or pleasure from human righteousness, yet reproves and enters into judgment. He is said to be in the heights of heaven, to have filled the houses of the wicked with good things, to hear the prayers of those who return, and to save the humble person.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: The addressee is accused by Eliphaz of taking pledges from his brother for nothing, stripping the naked, refusing water and bread to the weary and hungry, and sending widows away empty. He is also charged with saying that God cannot see through the thick darkness, and is told that snares, fear, darkness and floods surround him. He is urged to receive instruction and return to the Almighty.

l: wicked men, The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: Wicked men are described as having trodden an old way, being snatched away before their time, and having their foundation poured out like a stream. They told God to depart and asked what the Almighty could do for them. The righteous and innocent are said to be glad at their end, saying their remnant is consumed by fire.

l: Job's wickedness and iniquities, The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: Eliphaz declares the wickedness to be great and the iniquities endless. He cites taking pledges for nothing, stripping the naked, withholding water and bread, and sending widows away empty with the fatherless' arms broken. He presents these as the reason snares, sudden fear, darkness and floods surround the man.

l: repentance and return to God, The Book of Job, Chapter 22
s: Eliphaz urges the man to acquaint himself with God, be at peace, receive instruction from his mouth, and put away unrighteousness from his tents. He promises that returning to the Almighty will bring being built up, the Almighty as his treasure, delight in God, answered prayer, established decrees, light on his ways, and deliverance through clean hands.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 23
s: In Chapter 23, Job answers by saying his complaint is still rebellious because God's hand weighs heavily on him despite his groaning. He longs to find God and come to his seat so he can set out his cause and fill his mouth with arguments, believing God would listen rather than overpower him. Job says he cannot find God in the east, west, north, or south, yet God knows his way and, once he has been tried, Job expects to come out like gold. He affirms that he has kept God's way and treasured his commands, but he also describes God as unopposable and doing whatever he desires. Job ends by saying he is terrified and faint of heart before God, and that he was not cut off before the darkness came.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 23
s: Job answers by wishing he could find God and come to his seat to argue his case in order, confident that God would listen to him. He cannot locate God in any direction, but he insists God knows his way and that he will come out like gold after being tried. He claims he has held fast to God's steps, not turned from his commands, and valued God's words more than necessary food, yet he is terrified and faint of heart before God and was not cut off before the darkness.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 23
s: God is described by Job as having a heavy hand, as being impossible to find in the east, west, north, or south, and yet as knowing the way Job takes and trying him. Job says God stands alone, no one can oppose him, he does what his soul desires, and he performs what is appointed for Job. Job says God has made his heart faint and terrified him, though he believes God would not contend with him by sheer power but would listen.

l: Job's complaint, The Book of Job, Chapter 23
s: Job calls his complaint rebellious even today, because God's hand is heavy in spite of his groaning. He wants to set the complaint in order before God and fill his mouth with arguments, so that he might know God's answer and be delivered forever from his judge.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 24
s: In Chapter 24 the speaker asks why the Almighty does not set times of judgment and why those who know him do not see his days. He describes the wicked who move landmarks, seize flocks, drive off the donkey and ox of the fatherless and widow, and push the needy aside, so that the poor hide, scavenge for food like wild donkeys, go naked and exposed to the cold and rain, and labor hungry and thirsty for others. He says men groan in the city and the wounded cry out, yet God does not regard the folly. He then describes those who rebel against the light, including murderers, thieves and adulterers who act in darkness and fear the morning, and says they will be cursed, consumed by Sheol, forgotten, and broken like a tree. He adds that God preserves the mighty by his power and gives them security while watching their ways, until they are brought low and cut off like ears of grain, and he closes by challenging anyone to prove him a liar.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 24
s: The speaker asks why the Almighty does not lay up times of judgment and why those who know him do not see his days. He says God does not regard the folly of the wicked, yet also preserves the mighty by his power, gives them security, and watches their ways.

l: the wicked who oppress the poor, The Book of Job, Chapter 24
s: They remove landmarks, violently take flocks, drive away the donkey of the fatherless, take the widow's ox as a pledge, and pluck the fatherless from the breast. Others among them murder, steal, commit adultery, and dig into houses under cover of darkness. The speaker says they are like foam on the water, cursed, taken by Sheol, forgotten, and broken like a tree, though some are for a time preserved and exalted before being cut off like tops of grain.

l: the poor and needy, The Book of Job, Chapter 24
s: They are turned out of the way and hide themselves, scavenge like wild donkeys for food for their children, and glean the vineyard of the wicked. They lie naked in the cold, are wet with mountain showers, embrace the rock for shelter, carry sheaves while hungry, and tread wine presses while thirsty. Some are killed by the murderer, and those wounded groan and cry out.

l: God's delay of judgment on the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 24
s: The speaker questions why times of judgment are not laid up and seen by those who know God, noting that the cries of the wounded go unregarded. He says God instead preserves and secures the mighty for a while before they are brought low, and he challenges anyone to prove him a liar if this is not so.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 25
s: In Chapter 25, Bildad the Shuhite gives a brief reply in which he extols God's dominion, the fear that attends him, and the peace he makes in his high places. He asks whether God's armies can be counted and on whom his light does not arise. He then asks how man can be just with God, or how one born of a woman can be clean. He points out that even the moon lacks brightness and the stars are not pure in God's sight, concluding that man, a worm and the son of man, is far less so.

l: Bildad the Shuhite, The Book of Job, Chapter 25
s: Bildad the Shuhite answers with a short speech about God's greatness. He asks rhetorical questions about God's armies and light, and argues that man cannot be just or clean before God.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 25
s: God is described as having dominion and inspiring fear, and as making peace in his high places. His armies are said to be beyond counting, his light arises on everyone, and even the moon and stars are not bright or pure in his sight.

l: man, The Book of Job, Chapter 25
s: Man is described as born of a woman and as a worm, the son of man. He is judged far less bright and pure than the moon and stars, which themselves fall short in God's sight.

l: justice of man before God, The Book of Job, Chapter 25
s: Bildad questions whether man can be just with God, and whether one born of a woman can be clean. The implied answer is that he cannot, since even the moon and stars are not pure in God's sight and man is a worm.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 26
s: In Chapter 26, Job answers a previous speaker with sarcastic questions about how that speaker has helped the powerless, the weak, and the unwise, and whose spirit spoke through him. Job then describes God's dominion over the realm of the dead, where departed spirits tremble and Sheol and Abaddon lie uncovered before God. He praises God's power over creation: stretching the north over empty space, hanging the earth on nothing, binding the waters in clouds, setting a boundary on the waters, and shaking the pillars of heaven. Job says God stirs the sea, strikes through Rahab, adorns the heavens by his Spirit, and pierces the swift serpent. He concludes that all this is only the outskirts of God's ways, a small whisper, and that no one can understand the thunder of his power.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 26
s: Job answers with sarcasm, asking how the one he addresses has helped the powerless, saved the weak, and counseled the unwise, and whose spirit spoke through him. He then gives a long description of God's power over the dead, the earth, the waters, the heavens, and the sea. He concludes that people hear only a small whisper of God and cannot understand the thunder of his power.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 26
s: God is described by Job as having Sheol and Abaddon uncovered before him. He stretches out the north over empty space, hangs the earth on nothing, binds the waters in thick clouds, and sets a boundary on the waters at the confines of light and darkness. The pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke. He stirs the sea, strikes through Rahab, garnishes the heavens by his Spirit, and pierces the swift serpent with his hand.

l: one without power (the person Job addresses), The Book of Job, Chapter 26
s: In Job's sarcastic questions, the one without power is the person the other speaker is said to have helped, along with the one with no strength to be saved and the one with no wisdom to be counseled. Job's questions mock the claim of such help, asking to whom the words were uttered and whose spirit came out of the speaker.

l: God's power and ways, The Book of Job, Chapter 26
s: God's power is shown over the realm of the dead, the north, the earth, the waters and clouds, the boundary of light and darkness, the pillars of heaven, the sea, Rahab, and the swift serpent. Job calls these things only the outskirts of his ways, a small whisper that is heard. The thunder of his power, he says, no one can understand.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: In Chapter 27, Job resumes speaking and swears by the living God, whom he says has taken away his right and made his soul bitter, that he will not speak unrighteousness or deceit. He refuses to justify his friends and vows to hold fast to his righteousness and integrity until he dies. He wishes his enemy to be treated as the wicked and asks what hope the godless have when God takes their life, and whether God will hear their cry. Job then promises to teach about the hand of God, describing the portion of the wicked: their children die by the sword or go hungry, their widows do not mourn, and their riches pass to the just and innocent. He closes by describing the wicked man's sudden end, as terrors, a storm, and the east wind sweep him from his place while men clap and hiss at him.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: Job takes up his parable again and swears by the living God, who he says has taken away his right and made his soul bitter, that he will not speak unrighteousness or deceit. He refuses to justify his friends and declares he will hold fast to his righteousness until death. He then promises to teach about God's hand and describes the fate of the wicked.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: God is called the Almighty and is said by Job to have taken away his right and made his soul bitter. Job says God takes the life of the godless, may not hear their cry, and gives the wicked their portion, including the terrors, storm, and east wind that sweep the wicked man away.

l: wicked man, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: The wicked man's portion from the Almighty is that his many children are destined for the sword and go unsatisfied with bread, and his widows do not lament. His silver and clothing go to the just and innocent, his house is as fragile as a moth's or a watchman's booth, and he lies down rich but is suddenly gone. Terrors and a storm overtake him, and men clap and hiss him out of his place.

l: Job's friends, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: Job tells his friends he will never justify them. He says all of them have seen the matter themselves and asks why they have become altogether vain. He says he will teach them about the hand of God and will not conceal what is with the Almighty.

l: Job's integrity and oath of innocence, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: Job declares that until he dies he will not put away his integrity and will hold fast to his righteousness without letting it go. He says his heart will not reproach him as long as he lives.

l: fate of the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 27
s: Job says the godless have no hope when God cuts them off and takes their life, and God may not hear their cry or delight them. Their children face the sword and hunger, their survivors are buried in death without widows' lament, and their wealth passes to the just and innocent. They are swept away suddenly by terrors, a storm, and the east wind, and men clap and hiss at them.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 28
s: Chapter 28 opens by describing how man mines silver, gold, iron, copper, and precious stones, breaking open shafts, cutting channels in rock, overturning mountains, and bringing hidden things to light along paths no bird or beast knows. It then asks where wisdom and understanding can be found, answering that man does not know its price and it is not in the land of the living. The deep and the sea deny having it, and no gold, silver, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal, rubies, or topaz can purchase or equal it. Destruction and Death have only heard a rumor of it. God alone understands its way and place, having seen it when he set the wind, waters, rain, and lightning, and he tells man that the fear of the Lord is wisdom and departing from evil is understanding.

l: wisdom, The Book of Job, Chapter 28
s: Wisdom is asked about repeatedly as something that cannot be found in the land of the living, in the deep, or in the sea, and it is hidden from all living creatures. Its price is beyond gold, silver, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal, rubies, and topaz, and only God knows its place. It is finally declared to be the fear of the Lord.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 28
s: God is said to understand wisdom's way and know its place, looking to the ends of the earth and seeing under the whole sky. He established the wind's force, measured the waters, and made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning, and then saw, declared, established, and searched out wisdom. He tells man that the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

l: man, The Book of Job, Chapter 28
s: Man is shown as able to mine metals and gems, break open shafts, overturn mountains, and bring hidden things to light. Yet he does not know wisdom's price, and it is not found in the land of the living. God tells him that the fear of the Lord is wisdom and that departing from evil is understanding.

l: mining, The Book of Job, Chapter 28
s: Mining is described as man's pursuit of silver, gold, iron, copper, sapphires, and other precious things, carried out in remote shafts where workers hang far from people and swing back and forth. It sets an end to darkness and brings hidden things out to light. It serves as a contrast to wisdom, which no such searching or wealth can obtain.

l: fear of the Lord, The Book of Job, Chapter 28
s: The fear of the Lord is declared by God to man to be wisdom. It is paired with the statement that departing from evil is understanding.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 29
s: Job continues his parable by longing for the months of old, when God watched over him, his children were around him, and his life was blessed with abundance. He recalls the honor he received at the city gate, where young men hid, the aged stood, and princes and nobles fell silent. He explains that this esteem came from his righteousness: he delivered the poor, the fatherless, and the dying, caused the widow's heart to sing, and broke the jaws of the unrighteous. He remembers expecting to die in his own house with his glory renewed, and recalls how men waited for his counsel like rain, while he sat as chief and lived like a king who comforts mourners.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 29
s: Job longs for the past, recalling when God watched over him and his children were around him. He describes himself as a man who delivered the poor, the fatherless, and the widow, wore righteousness and justice like a robe, and was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. He broke the jaws of the unrighteous, expected to die in his own house, and sat as chief among men, comforting mourners.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 29
s: God is remembered as having watched over Job in the months of old, his lamp shining on Job's head and lighting Job's way through darkness. His friendship was in Job's tent, and the Almighty was with Job then.

l: poor and needy (those Job helped), The Book of Job, Chapter 29
s: The poor who cried, the fatherless with no helper, and the one ready to perish were delivered by Job. The perishing one's blessing came on Job, and the widow's heart was caused to sing for joy. Job was a father to the needy and investigated the cause of those he did not know.

l: men (Job's listeners), The Book of Job, Chapter 29
s: Young men saw Job and hid themselves, the aged rose and stood, and princes and nobles fell silent, hands on their mouths and tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths. They listened, waited, and kept silent for his counsel, did not speak again after his words, and waited for him as for the rain. When they lacked confidence he smiled on them, and they did not reject the light of his face.

l: Job's former prosperity and honor, The Book of Job, Chapter 29
s: Job recalls a time when his steps were washed with butter and the rock poured out streams of oil for him. He had a seat at the city gate, esteem from all ranks, and the blessing of those he helped. He expected his glory to stay fresh and his bow to be renewed, his root spread to the waters, and his days to be many as the sand.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 30
s: In Chapter 30, Job laments his fall from honor. He describes how men younger than himself, whose fathers he once thought unworthy to work with his sheep dogs, now mock him; they are portrayed as gaunt outcasts who live in wastelands and were driven out of the land. These men make Job their song and byword, spit in his face, and press destruction upon him. Job then turns to God, saying he cries out and gets no answer, that God has become cruel and persecutes him, and that he expects death. He ends by recalling that he wept for the troubled and needy, yet evil and darkness came when he looked for good and light, leaving him mourning, ill, and isolated.

l: Job's suffering and affliction, The Book of Job, Chapter 30
s: Job's affliction is described as days of affliction that have taken hold of him, with his soul poured out and his bones pierced and gnawed by pain that gives no rest at night. His garment is disfigured, his skin grows black and peels, and his bones burn with heat. Terrors chase his honor like the wind, and he goes mourning, a brother to jackals and a companion to ostriches.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 31
s: In Chapter 31, Job concludes his defense with a series of oaths declaring his innocence. He says he made a covenant with his eyes against lust, and denies falsehood, adultery, despising his servants, withholding help from the poor, widow and fatherless, trusting in gold, worshiping the sun or moon, rejoicing at an enemy's ruin, turning away travelers, hiding transgressions, and wronging his land. For each claim he names a self-imposed penalty, such as losing his harvest, his wife being given to others, or his arm being broken. He acknowledges that God sees his ways and that calamity from God terrifies him. He ends by demanding that the Almighty answer him and write out an indictment, which he would wear like a crown, and the narrator notes that the words of Job are ended.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 31
s: Job speaks his final defense, claiming he has kept a covenant with his eyes and has been faithful, just, generous to servants, the poor, the widow and the fatherless, and hospitable to strangers. He invites severe penalties on himself if any of his claims are false, and challenges the Almighty to answer him. He says he would present the number of his steps to God like a prince, and the chapter closes with the note that his words are ended.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 31
s: God is described by Job as the one who sees his ways and counts all his steps, who sends calamity on the unrighteous, and who made both Job and his servants in the womb. Job says he fears God's calamity and majesty, and that sin would deny the God above. Job demands that the Almighty answer him and that the accuser write an indictment, but God does not respond in this unit.

l: Job's integrity and oath of innocence, The Book of Job, Chapter 31
s: Job swears a long series of conditional oaths ("if I have...") denying lust, deceit, adultery, mistreatment of servants, neglect of the poor, trust in wealth, idolatry of the sun and moon, gloating over an enemy, inhospitality, concealed sin, and exploiting his land. Each is paired with a curse he accepts if guilty, and he signs his statement and offers to bear any indictment as a crown. This forms his final assertion that he is blameless.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: Job's three friends stop answering him because he remains righteous in his own eyes. Elihu the son of Barachel, the Buzite, becomes angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the three friends for condemning Job without finding an answer. Elihu explains that he held back because the others were older, but argues that understanding comes from the Spirit of the Almighty rather than from age or greatness. He declares that he will now give his own answer, saying he is full of words and ready to burst like a wineskin. He vows to show no partiality and to give no flattering titles, lest his Maker take him away.

l: Elihu, The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: Elihu waited to speak because the three friends were older, then became angry when they had no answer for Job. He says he is young but that the Spirit of the Almighty gives understanding, and he resolves to give his own opinion. He claims he is full of words, will speak impartially, and will not flatter anyone, for fear that his Maker would take him away.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: Job is no longer answered by his three friends because he is righteous in his own eyes. Elihu is angry at him for justifying himself rather than God. Elihu also says that none of the friends convinced Job or answered his words.

l: three friends (Job's three friends), The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: The three friends cease to answer Job, who remains righteous in his own eyes. Elihu is angry at them because they found no answer yet condemned Job. He says they are amazed, have no word left to say, and should not claim that God, not man, will refute Job.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: God is the one Elihu says Job justified himself against, which provoked Elihu's wrath. Elihu says the Spirit of the Almighty gives people understanding, and he refers to God as his Maker, who would soon take him away if he flattered anyone.

l: wrath (Elihu's wrath), The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: Elihu's wrath is kindled against Job because Job justified himself rather than God. It is also kindled against the three friends because they found no answer yet condemned Job. It is mentioned again when Elihu sees that the three men have no answer.

l: age and wisdom, The Book of Job, Chapter 32
s: Elihu says he first thought days and many years should teach wisdom, which is why he held back as the younger man. He then asserts that a spirit in man, the Spirit of the Almighty, gives understanding, and that it is not the great who are wise nor the aged who understand justice.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: The speaker addresses Job directly, asking him to listen and answer, and affirms that he too was made by God's Spirit and formed from clay, so he is no terror to Job. He recalls Job's claims that he is clean and innocent and that God treats him as an enemy, and replies that Job is not just in this because God is greater than man and owes no account of his matters. He explains that God speaks to people through dreams, visions, and the chastening pain of a sickbed, in order to turn man from his purpose and keep his soul from the pit. If an angel or interpreter, one in a thousand, shows a man what is right, God is gracious, finds a ransom, restores his flesh and righteousness, and brings him to sing of his sin and redemption. The speaker closes by urging Job to listen, to answer if he has anything to say since he desires to justify him, or otherwise to stay silent and be taught wisdom.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: Job is addressed directly and told to listen, to set his words in order and answer, and to hold his peace if he has nothing to say. The speaker quotes Job as having said that he is clean, without disobedience, innocent, and that God finds occasions against him, counts him an enemy, puts his feet in the stocks, and marks his paths. He is told he is not just in this and is offered the chance to be justified or taught wisdom.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: God is described as greater than man and as not giving account of any of his matters. He speaks once, even twice, to man through dreams and visions, opens men's ears and seals their instruction, and keeps a man's soul from the pit. He is gracious to the man helped by an interpreter, declares he has found a ransom, restores the man's righteousness, and does all these things two or three times with a man to bring his soul back from the pit and into the light of the living.

l: Elihu, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: The speaker opens by asking Job to hear his words, saying they come from the uprightness of his heart and are spoken sincerely. He says that the Spirit of God made him and that he is formed out of clay like Job, so his terror and pressure need not weigh on Job. He answers Job's claims by declaring that God is greater than man, describes how God deals with people, and ends by saying he desires to justify Job or else teach him wisdom.

l: man, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: Man is portrayed as often paying no attention when God speaks. God opens his ears, withdraws him from his purpose, hides pride from him, and keeps his soul from the pit and his life from perishing by the sword. If he is shown what is right and ransomed, he is restored, prays and is received, sees God's face with joy, and sings before men of his sin.

l: God's communication through dreams and visions, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: God is said to speak once, even twice, though man pays no attention. In a dream or night vision, when deep sleep falls on men, he opens their ears and seals their instruction. The purpose is to withdraw man from his purpose, hide pride from him, and keep his soul from the pit and from death by the sword.

l: suffering and chastening of a man on his sickbed, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: A man is chastened with pain on his bed and continual strife in his bones, so that his life abhors bread and his soul dainty food. His flesh is consumed away until it cannot be seen, his unseen bones stick out, and his soul draws near to the pit and his life to the destroyers.

l: Job's claim of innocence, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: Job's claim, as quoted by the speaker, is that he is clean, without disobedience, innocent, and without iniquity, and that God nonetheless treats him as an enemy. The speaker answers that in this Job is not just, because God is greater than man and owes no account of his matters.

l: restoration and redemption of a man, The Book of Job, Chapter 33
s: If an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand, shows a man what is right, God is gracious, says to deliver him from the pit, and declares he has found a ransom. The man's flesh becomes fresher than a child's, he returns to the days of his youth, prays and is favored, sees God's face with joy, and has his righteousness restored. He then sings before men confessing his sin and says that God has redeemed his soul and his life will see the light.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: In Chapter 34, Elihu addresses the wise men and men of understanding, asking them to weigh his words and choose together what is right. He quotes Job as claiming to be righteous while God has taken away his right, and accuses Job of keeping company with the wicked and saying it profits nothing to delight in God. Elihu insists that God cannot do wickedness or pervert justice, that He owes no one an account for governing the earth, and that He sees all human ways, breaks the mighty, and hears the cry of the poor. He argues that no one can condemn God when He gives quietness, and that no one has truly told God they would repent. He closes by saying Job speaks without knowledge and wishes Job were tried to the end for adding rebellion to his sin.

l: Elihu, The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: Elihu calls on the wise men to judge his words and then argues at length that God is just, quoting and rebuking Job's statements. He accuses Job of speaking without knowledge, of adding rebellion to his sin, and of multiplying words against God, and wishes that Job were tried to the end.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: Job is quoted by Elihu as having said that he is righteous, that God has taken away his right, that he is called a liar despite being without disobedience, and that it profits a man nothing to delight in God. Elihu charges him with drinking scorn like water, walking with wicked men, speaking without wisdom, clapping his hands among them, and adding rebellion to his sin.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: In Elihu's account, God will not do wickedness or pervert justice, and he repays each man according to his ways. No one appointed him over the earth, and if he withdrew his spirit and breath all flesh would perish. He sees every step, has no darkness where evildoers can hide, breaks mighty men and sets others in their place, strikes the wicked in the open, and hears the cry of the poor and afflicted. He rules over nations and individuals alike so that the godless may not reign.

l: wise men (Elihu's audience), The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: Elihu addresses them as wise men and men of understanding with knowledge, asking them to listen, to test his words as the palate tastes food, and to choose with him what is right. He expects them to agree that Job speaks without knowledge and that his words lack wisdom.

l: God's justice, The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: Elihu insists that God's justice is beyond question: far be it from God to do wickedness, and he will not pervert justice. He gives each man the result of his work, shows no partiality between princes, the rich, and the poor, and needs no further inquiry into a man before judging. Elihu asks whether one who hates justice could govern, and says God overturns the wicked and hears the cries of the afflicted.

l: Job's complaint against God (Job's claim of righteousness), The Book of Job, Chapter 34
s: Elihu restates Job's complaint as the claim that Job is righteous, that God has taken away his right, and that his wound is incurable though he is without disobedience. Elihu rejects it, saying God cannot act unjustly, that no one has actually confessed guilt and promised to do no more, and that Job's words amount to rebellion against God.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 35
s: In Chapter 35, Elihu continues his speech by answering Job and his companions. He challenges Job's claim that his righteousness exceeds God's and his question about what profit there is in not sinning. Elihu tells Job to look at the skies to see that God is higher than he is, so that neither sin nor righteousness affects God but only other people. He says people cry out under oppression yet do not seek God their Maker, so God does not answer the cry of the proud and does not hear an empty cry. He concludes that Job speaks empty talk and multiplies words without knowledge.

l: Elihu, The Book of Job, Chapter 35
s: Elihu answers Job and his companions, questioning whether Job thinks it right to claim that his righteousness is more than God's. He argues that human sin and righteousness do not affect God, that God does not hear an empty cry, and that Job opens his mouth with empty talk and words without knowledge.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 35
s: Job is charged by Elihu with saying that his righteousness is more than God's and with asking what profit he has more than if he had sinned. Elihu says Job says he does not see God, and that he speaks empty talk and multiplies words without knowledge.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 35
s: God is presented as higher than the skies and than humans, unaffected by their sin or righteousness, and as the Maker who gives songs in the night and makes people wiser than the animals and birds. He does not answer the cry of those who are proud and evil, will not hear an empty cry, and has not visited in anger nor greatly regarded arrogance.

l: righteousness, The Book of Job, Chapter 35
s: Elihu says Job claims that his righteousness is more than God's. He argues that a righteous person gives God nothing and that God receives nothing from his hand, and that righteousness profits only other people, a son of man.

l: sin and wickedness, The Book of Job, Chapter 35
s: Elihu says that sinning and multiplying transgressions have no effect against God and do nothing to him. He says a person's wickedness may hurt other people, and that the pride of evil men is the reason the cries of the oppressed go unanswered.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: Elihu continues speaking, asking for patience as he claims to speak on God's behalf and to declare his Maker righteous.
