He says God is mighty and despises no one, that he denies the wicked life, gives justice to the afflicted, and exalts the righteous, and that when people are bound in affliction he shows them their pride and calls them to turn from iniquity. Those who listen prosper, while those who do not perish without knowledge. Elihu then turns to the person he addresses, warning him against being enticed by riches or bribes, against desiring the night, and against choosing iniquity over affliction. He closes by praising God's greatness, who draws up water into rain, spreads the clouds, thunders, and commands the lightning, which judges peoples and gives food in abundance.

l: Elihu, The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: Elihu continues speaking, asking for a little more patience because he still has words on God's behalf. He claims his knowledge comes from afar, that his words are not false, and that one perfect in knowledge is with his listener. He argues that God is just, warns his addressee, and ends by praising God's power over the weather.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: God is described as mighty in strength of understanding, despising no one, withholding life from the wicked, giving justice to the afflicted, and keeping his eyes on the righteous. He opens the ears of the afflicted to instruction and commands them to turn from iniquity, rewarding those who listen with prosperity and letting those who don't perish. He is exalted in power, an unmatched teacher, answerable to no one, great and unknowable, with unsearchable years. He draws up water for rain, spreads the clouds, covers the bottom of the sea, and commands the lightning to strike its mark.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: The person Elihu addresses is told he is full of the judgment of the wicked, with judgment and justice taking hold of him. He is warned not to let riches entice him to wrath, not to let a large bribe turn him aside, and not to desire the night. Elihu says God would have allured him out of distress into a wide place with a full table, and that he has chosen iniquity rather than affliction. He is also told to remember to magnify God's work.

l: the wicked, The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: God does not preserve the life of the wicked. Those godless in heart lay up anger and do not cry for help when God binds them, and they die in youth, their lives perishing among the unclean. Those who refuse to listen to God's instruction perish by the sword and die without knowledge.

l: the righteous, The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: God does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, and he sets them with kings on the throne forever, exalted. If they are bound in fetters and afflictions, he shows them their work and their proud transgressions, opens their ears to instruction, and commands them to turn from iniquity. If they listen and serve him, they spend their days in prosperity and their years in pleasures.

l: rain and clouds (God's weather), The Book of Job, Chapter 36
s: God draws up the drops of water, which distill as rain from his vapor, and the skies pour it down abundantly on man. No one can understand the spreading of the clouds or the thunderings of his pavilion. By these means he judges the people and gives food in abundance, and the noise of the storm tells about him, as the livestock also do.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 37
s: In Chapter 37, a speaker describes God's power as seen in nature, beginning with his heart trembling at the sound of God's voice. He portrays God's thundering voice and lightning reaching the ends of the earth, and God commanding snow, rain, storm, cold, and ice, so that animals take shelter and people are made to know his work. The speaker says God directs the clouds for correction, for his land, or for loving kindness. He then addresses Job directly, telling him to stand still and consider God's wondrous works, and asks a series of questions about whether Job understands the clouds, the lightning, or can spread out the sky. He closes by saying the Almighty cannot be reached, is exalted in power, and does not oppress in justice and great righteousness, so men revere him and he does not regard those who are wise of heart.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 37
s: God thunders marvelously with his voice, commands snow, rain, storm and ice, and loads and turns the clouds by his guidance to do whatever he commands. He is described as perfect in knowledge, as exalted in power, and as one who will not oppress in justice and great righteousness. Men revere him, and he does not regard any who are wise of heart.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 37
s: Job is addressed directly and told to listen, stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God. He is asked whether he knows how God controls the clouds and lightning, knows the workings of the clouds, or can spread out the sky with God. These questions imply that he cannot.

l: thunder and lightning (God's voice), The Book of Job, Chapter 37
s: God's voice sounds as thunder and roars under the whole sky, and his lightning goes to the ends of the earth. The thunder holds nothing back when heard, and God thunders marvelously. The speaker's heart trembles at it, and he calls on listeners to hear the noise of the voice.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 38
s: In Chapter 38 the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, challenging him as one who darkens counsel by words without knowledge and telling him to brace himself to be questioned. The LORD asks where Job was when the earth's foundations were laid, when the morning stars sang, and when the sea was shut in with doors and bounds. He then asks whether Job has commanded the morning, entered the springs of the sea, seen the gates of death, or knows the way to the dwelling of light and darkness. The LORD questions Job about snow, hail, lightning, rain, dew, ice, and frost, and about binding the Pleiades and Orion and knowing the laws of the heavens. The chapter closes with questions about who gives wisdom and who counts the clouds, and about who hunts prey for the lioness and provides food for the raven and its young.

l: the LORD, The Book of Job, Chapter 38
s: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, telling him to brace himself to be questioned and to answer. He describes himself as the one who laid the earth's foundations, shut the sea within bounds, sends rain to empty wilderness, and provides prey for lions and ravens, and he challenges Job to match these works.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 38
s: Job is addressed by the LORD as one who darkens counsel by words without knowledge and is told to brace himself like a man. He is met with a long series of questions about creation, the sea, light, weather, the stars, and animals, none of which he answers in this unit, and the questions imply he was not present and lacks the knowledge and power they describe.

l: earth, The Book of Job, Chapter 38
s: The earth is described as having foundations laid by the LORD, with measures determined, a line stretched on it, and a cornerstone set while the morning stars sang. Dawn is said to take hold of its ends and shake the wicked out of it, and Job is asked whether he has comprehended its width. Rain falls on its wilderness where no man lives, making tender grass grow.

l: the deep, The Book of Job, Chapter 38
s: The sea is said to have broken out as from a womb, and the LORD shut it up with doors, made clouds its garment, and wrapped it in thick darkness. He set its bound and bars and told it, 'You may come here, but no further,' so its proud waves are stopped. Job is asked whether he has entered the springs of the sea, and the surface of the deep is said to freeze hard like stone.

l: weather phenomena, The Book of Job, Chapter 38
s: Snow and hail are described as stored in the LORD's storehouses, reserved for times of trouble, battle, and war. Lightning, the east wind, floods, thunderstorms, rain, dew, ice, frost, and clouds are all presented as things Job cannot direct, count, or explain. Rain is said to fall even where no man lives, satisfying desolate ground and making grass grow.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: In Chapter 39, the speaker poses a series of rhetorical questions about wild animals to show the limits of human knowledge and control. He asks about mountain goats and does giving birth, the wild donkey living free in the wilderness, the wild ox that will not serve or be harnessed, the ostrich that neglects her eggs and lacks wisdom, the powerful war horse that charges into battle, and the hawk and eagle that soar and nest on high cliffs. Each creature is presented as living by capacities and instincts that the listener did not give and cannot command.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: God is the implied speaker who questions whether the listener can govern the wild creatures, and says he made the wilderness and salt land the wild donkey's home. The text states that God deprived the ostrich of wisdom and did not impart understanding to her.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: Job is not named in this unit. The listener addressed with questions such as 'Do you know...' and 'Can you...' is asked whether he understands or controls the birth, freedom, strength, and flight of wild animals.

l: wild donkey, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: The wild donkey is set free, with the wilderness and salt land made his home. He scorns the city's tumult and the driver's shouting, and ranges the mountains searching for every green thing.

l: wild ox, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: The wild ox is described as unwilling to serve or stay by a feeding trough. He cannot be held in the furrow with a harness, and the listener is asked whether he would trust him with labor, seed, or grain despite his great strength.

l: ostrich, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: The ostrich waves her wings proudly but leaves her eggs on the earth and forgets that feet or wild animals may crush them. She treats her young harshly, is without fear, and lacks wisdom because God deprived her of it, yet when she lifts herself up she scorns the horse and rider.

l: horse, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: The horse is described as given might and a quivering mane, leaping like a locust with an awesome snort. He paws the valley, rejoices in his strength, mocks fear, does not turn from the sword, and snorts 'Aha!' at the trumpet as he smells the battle from afar.

l: eagle, The Book of Job, Chapter 39
s: The eagle mounts up at no command of the listener and makes his nest on high, dwelling on the cliff and the stronghold. From there he spies prey with far-seeing eyes, and his young suck up blood: where the slain are, there he is.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 40
s: In Chapter 40, the LORD challenges Job, asking whether one who argues with the Almighty will answer. Job replies that he is of small account, lays his hand on his mouth, and says he will proceed no further. Out of the whirlwind the LORD tells Job to brace himself, asks whether he will annul his judgment and condemn him to be justified, and challenges him to deck himself with majesty, bring down the proud and the wicked, so that the LORD would admit his own right hand can save him. The LORD then directs Job to behemoth, which he made as well as Job, describing its grass-eating, its strength, bones like bronze and iron, its calm in the marsh and the swelling Jordan, and asking whether anyone can capture it.

l: the LORD, The Book of Job, Chapter 40
s: The LORD answers Job, first asking whether one who argues with God will answer, then speaking out of the whirlwind to tell Job to brace himself and answer his questions. He challenges Job to match his arm and thunder, to humble the proud and crush the wicked, and says he would then admit Job's right hand can save him. He points Job to behemoth, which he made, and describes its strength.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 40
s: Job answers the LORD by saying he is of small account, lays his hand on his mouth, and says he has spoken once and twice but will proceed no further. He is then told to brace himself, is questioned about annulling the LORD's judgment and condemning him to be justified, and is challenged to show an arm and voice like God's. He is directed to consider behemoth.

l: behemoth, The Book of Job, Chapter 40
s: Behemoth is presented as a creature the LORD made as well as Job, eating grass like an ox, with strength in its thighs, a tail like a cedar, bones like tubes of bronze and limbs like bars of iron. It is called the chief of the ways of God, and its maker gives it its sword. It lies under the lotus trees and reeds, does not tremble when a river overflows, and the text asks whether anyone can take it on watch or pierce its nose with a snare.

l: judgment of God, The Book of Job, Chapter 40
s: The LORD asks Job whether he will even annul his judgment or condemn him so that Job may be justified. This frames Job's earlier argument as a challenge to God's judgment, which Job is asked to answer for.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 41
s: In Chapter 41, the speaker challenges the addressee with a series of rhetorical questions about Leviathan, asking whether he can catch, tame, sell, or fight it. The speaker declares that no one is fierce enough to stir Leviathan up, and asks who then can stand before the speaker, since everything under the heavens belongs to the speaker. The speaker then describes Leviathan's limbs, strength, and frame in detail: his tightly sealed scales, fiery breath, firm heart, and terrifying jaws. Weapons of every kind fail against him, and he churns the deep like a boiling pot. The chapter ends by calling Leviathan without equal on earth, made without fear, and king over all the sons of pride.

l: leviathan, The Book of Job, Chapter 41
s: Leviathan is described as a creature that cannot be caught with a hook, cord, or rope, will not plead or make a covenant, and cannot be tamed or traded. His strong scales, flashing eyes, fiery breath, stone-hard heart, and terrifying teeth are detailed, and swords, spears, arrows, and clubs are counted as nothing to him. He stirs the deep to boil, has no equal on earth, is made without fear, and is king over all the sons of pride.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 41
s: The speaker questions the addressee about Leviathan, stressing that no one can stir him up and asking who can stand before the speaker. He asserts that no one has first given to him so that he must repay, and that everything under the heavens is his. He declares he will not keep silent about Leviathan's limbs, strength, and frame, and describes them at length.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 41
s: Job is addressed with a series of rhetorical questions about whether he could catch, bind, sell, or fight Leviathan. He is told to lay his hand on the creature, remember the battle, and do so no more, and that even the sight of Leviathan casts one down. He is thereby challenged to consider who can stand before the speaker.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: In Chapter 42, Job answers the LORD, acknowledging that the LORD can do all things and that he himself spoke of things he did not understand. He says he had heard of the LORD by hearing but now sees him, and he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD then tells Eliphaz the Temanite that his wrath is kindled against him and his two friends because they did not speak rightly of him as Job did, and directs them to offer seven bulls and seven rams as a burnt offering while Job prays for them. After the friends obey, the LORD accepts Job and restores his prosperity at twice what he had before. Job's relatives and acquaintances comfort him and give him gifts, he has fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, a thousand female donkeys, seven sons and three daughters, and he lives one hundred forty more years before dying old and full of days.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: Job answers the LORD, confessing that he spoke of things he did not understand, and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD calls him his servant, says he spoke rightly, and accepts his prayer for his three friends. He is restored with twice his former wealth, has seven sons and three daughters, lives one hundred forty more years, sees four generations, and dies old and full of days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: The LORD is acknowledged by Job as able to do all things, with no purpose of his restrained. He expresses wrath against Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly of him as Job did, commands them to offer a burnt offering, and accepts Job. He restores Job's prosperity at twice the former amount and blesses his latter end more than his beginning.

l: Eliphaz the Temanite, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: The LORD addresses Eliphaz, telling him that his wrath is kindled against him and his two friends because they did not speak rightly of him as Job did. Eliphaz goes with Bildad and Zophar and does what the LORD commanded.

l: Bildad the Shuhite, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: Bildad is included in the LORD's wrath against Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly of him. He goes with Eliphaz and Zophar and does what the LORD commanded.

l: Zophar the Naamathite, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: Zophar is included in the LORD's wrath against Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly of him. He goes with Eliphaz and Bildad and does what the LORD commanded.

l: friends (Job's three friends), The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: The LORD tells Eliphaz that his wrath is kindled against him and his two friends because they did not speak rightly of him as Job did. They take seven bulls and seven rams to Job and offer a burnt offering, and Job prays for them so the LORD will not deal with them according to their folly.

l: burnt offering (offered by Job's friends), The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: The LORD commands Job's friends to take seven bulls and seven rams and offer them as a burnt offering. They do as commanded, and Job prays for them, after which the LORD accepts Job.

l: Job's restored prosperity, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: When Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his prosperity and gives him twice as much as before. He has fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, a thousand female donkeys, seven sons and three daughters. His relatives and acquaintances eat with him, comfort him, and each give him a piece of money and a gold ring.

l: Job's repentance, The Book of Job, Chapter 42
s: Job says he had heard of the LORD by the hearing of the ear but now his eye sees him. Therefore he abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes, having uttered things he did not understand.

l: The Lamentations of Jeremiah, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 laments the desolation of Jerusalem, pictured as a once-populous city now sitting solitary like a widow and slave. Her lovers and friends have betrayed her, Judah has gone into captivity, the roads to Zion mourn, and her gates, priests, and virgins suffer. The text attributes her affliction to the LORD, who acted because of her many transgressions, while her adversaries prosper, mock her, and enter her sanctuary. Jerusalem speaks in her own voice, describing her pain, confessing she has rebelled, and asking the LORD to look on her distress. She ends by asking that her enemies' wickedness come before the LORD and that they be treated as she has been.

l: Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem is portrayed as a once-great city now solitary, widowed, enslaved, weeping, and without a comforter, betrayed by her lovers and friends. She is called unclean because of her grievous sin, and in her own voice she confesses rebellion, describes her sorrow, and asks the LORD to see her distress and deal with her enemies as he dealt with her.

l: LORD, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD is said to have afflicted Jerusalem in the day of his fierce anger for the multitude of her transgressions, sending fire into her bones, spreading a net for her feet, and treading her as in a wine press. Jerusalem acknowledges that he is righteous, appeals to him to look and see her affliction, and asks him to bring the day he proclaimed against her enemies.

l: adversary and enemy (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem's adversaries have become the head and prosper, mocking her desolations, spreading their hand on her pleasant things, and entering her sanctuary, which the LORD had forbidden to the nations. They are glad of her trouble, and Jerusalem asks that her enemies be made like her and that their wickedness come before the LORD.

l: people of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The people sigh and seek bread, giving up their pleasant things for food, while the priests and elders gave up the spirit in the city seeking food. Princes have lost strength like deer without pasture, the mighty and young men are crushed, and the virgins and young men have gone into captivity.

l: captivity (exile of Judah), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: Judah has gone into captivity because of affliction and great servitude, dwelling among the nations and finding no rest, with persecutors overtaking her. Her young children, virgins, and young men are described as having gone into captivity before the adversary.

l: sins of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 1
s: The chapter says Jerusalem grievously sinned, became unclean, and did not remember her latter end, with her filthiness in her skirts. The LORD afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions, which are pictured as a yoke bound by his hand on her neck, and she confesses that she rebelled against his commandment.

l: The Lamentations of Jeremiah, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 describes the Lord acting in anger as an enemy against the daughter of Zion, Jerusalem, Israel, and Jacob. He throws down strongholds, palaces, the tabernacle, altar, and sanctuary, and causes solemn assembly and Sabbath to be forgotten, while king, priest, and prophets are despised or left without vision. The speaker weeps over the suffering of young children and infants who faint from hunger in the streets, and says the false prophets did not expose Zion's iniquity. Passersby and enemies mock the city and rejoice over its fall, and the chapter ends with a call to Zion to cry out to the Lord, followed by a prayer asking him to look at the slain, the starving, and the terrors he has called upon the people.

l: LORD, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The Lord is portrayed as acting in anger like an enemy: he covers Zion with a cloud, swallows up dwellings and strongholds, withdraws his right hand from before the enemy, and casts off his altar and sanctuary. He has done what he planned and fulfilled the word he commanded in days of old, without pity. At the end he is called upon to look and see whom he has treated this way.

l: daughter of Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The daughter of Zion is covered with a cloud of the Lord's anger, has her wall targeted for destruction, and has wrath poured out like fire in her tent. Her elders sit silent in dust and sackcloth, her breach is said to be as big as the sea, and she is told to cry out to the Lord day and night.

l: Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: In Zion the Lord has caused solemn assembly and Sabbath to be forgotten and has despised the king and the priest. Its elders mourn, and the wall of the daughter of Zion is urged to let tears run like a river.

l: Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Jerusalem's virgins hang their heads to the ground, and its daughter is mocked by all who pass by, who ask whether this is the city called the perfection of beauty and the joy of the whole earth. Its children and infants swoon in the streets, and the speaker asks what could comfort it.

l: Israel, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Israel's beauty is cast down from heaven to earth, and the Lord cuts off all the horn of Israel in fierce anger. He swallows up Israel and all her palaces, and he is said to have become as an enemy.

l: Jacob, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: All the dwellings of Jacob are swallowed up without pity, and the Lord burns up Jacob like a flaming fire that devours all around.

l: adversary and enemy (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The enemy is given the walls of Zion's palaces by the Lord and makes a noise in the Lord's house as on a solemn assembly day. Enemies open their mouths, hiss, gnash their teeth, and claim to have swallowed Zion up; the Lord has caused them to rejoice and has exalted the horn of her adversaries.

l: children and infants (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: Young children and infants swoon in the city's streets, asking their mothers for grain and wine, and their souls are poured out into their mothers' bosoms. They faint from hunger at the head of every street, and Zion is urged to lift up her hands to the Lord for their lives. The prayer adds that women have eaten their offspring.

l: destruction of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 2
s: The destruction includes the casting down of strongholds, palaces, gates, bars, walls, the tabernacle, and the sanctuary, along with famine and slaughter by the sword of youth, old men, virgins, and young men. The text presents it as the Lord's doing in the day of his anger, with no one escaping or remaining, and the speaker grieves it with failing eyes and a troubled heart.

l: The Lamentations of Jeremiah, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3 the speaker, a man who has seen affliction, describes how the LORD has afflicted him: walling him in, breaking his bones, shooting him with arrows, and making him a song of derision to his people. He then turns to hope, recalling that the LORD's loving kindnesses and mercies are new every morning, that the LORD is good to those who wait for him, and that he will not cast off forever. He reflects that the Lord does not afflict willingly and urges himself and others to search their ways, return to the LORD, and confess transgression. He weeps over the destruction of the daughter of his people and describes enemies who chased him without cause and cast him into a dungeon. He recalls that the LORD heard his cry and redeemed his life, and he asks the LORD to judge his cause and repay his enemies according to the work of their hands.

l: LORD, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD is first described as the one who afflicted the speaker, shutting out his prayer and covering himself with a cloud. He is then affirmed as good, merciful and faithful, one who does not cast off forever, does not afflict willingly, and who heard the speaker's cry from the dungeon, redeemed his life, and is asked to judge his cause and pay back his enemies.

l: the speaker (the man who has seen affliction), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The speaker describes being led into darkness, walled in, broken, and made a mark for the LORD's arrow, and he says his strength and expectation have perished. He then recalls the LORD's mercies and takes hope, declares the LORD his portion, and urges repentance. He also recounts being hunted by enemies and thrown into a dungeon, calling on the LORD's name, being told not to be afraid, and being redeemed, and he asks for judgment on his enemies.

l: the speaker's affliction, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The affliction is portrayed as the LORD's doing: aged flesh, broken bones, bitterness, heavy chains, blocked paths, and arrows in the kidneys. The speaker's soul remembers it and is bowed down, and he asks the LORD to remember it. It is not presented as endless, since the LORD does not afflict willingly and will have compassion.

l: hope in the LORD's mercies and faithfulness, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The speaker turns to hope by recalling that the LORD's loving kindnesses keep us from being consumed and that his mercies are new every morning. He affirms that great is the LORD's faithfulness, that the LORD is good to those who wait for him, and that it is good to hope and quietly wait for his salvation.

l: enemies (the speaker's enemies), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The enemies open their mouths wide against the people and chase the speaker like a bird without cause. They cut off his life in the dungeon and cast a stone on him, and they plot against him all day long and mock him in song. The speaker says the LORD has seen their vengeance and will pay them back, giving them hardness of heart and destroying them from under the LORD's heavens.

l: speakers (the lamenting community), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 3
s: The speaker's people make him a derision and a song all day long. He weeps without ceasing over the destruction of the daughter of his people, and the people as a whole confess that they have transgressed and rebelled, that they have been covered with anger, and that they have been made refuse among the peoples, facing terror, the pit, devastation and destruction.

l: The Lamentations of Jeremiah, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 laments the ruin of Zion and its people after the siege of Jerusalem. The once precious sons of Zion, nobles and delicate women are now starving, blackened and desolate, and children go without bread while mothers have boiled their own children for food. The text declares that the LORD has poured out his wrath and kindled a fire in Zion, and that the sins of the prophets and priests, who shed the blood of the just, are the cause. The people, wandering polluted and shunned, were hunted and captured by pursuers, including the anointed of the LORD, who was taken in their pits. The chapter ends by telling the daughter of Edom that the cup will pass to her and her sins will be uncovered, while the punishment of the daughter of Zion is accomplished and she will not be carried into captivity again.

l: speakers (the lamenting community), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The daughter of my people is described as having become cruel, like ostriches in the wilderness, and her iniquity is said to be greater than the sin of Sodom. Her destruction is marked by mothers boiling their own children for food.

l: Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: Zion has a fire kindled in it by the LORD that devours its foundations. Its daughter's punishment for iniquity is declared accomplished, and she will not be carried away into captivity again.

l: sons of Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The precious sons of Zion, once comparable to fine gold, are now esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of a potter's hands. Their nobles, once purer than snow and ruddy like rubies, now have appearances blacker than coal, with skin clinging to their bones and withered like wood.

l: LORD, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD has accomplished his wrath and poured out his fierce anger, kindling a fire in Zion that devoured its foundations. His anger scattered the people, and he will no longer pay attention to them. His anointed, the breath of their nostrils, was taken in the pits of their pursuers.

l: Edom, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The daughter of Edom, who dwells in the land of Uz, is told to rejoice and be glad, but the cup will pass to her also. She will be drunken and make herself naked, and the LORD will visit her iniquity and uncover her sins.

l: prophets and priests (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The ruin is attributed to the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed the blood of the just in the middle of the city. They wander as blind men in the streets, so polluted with blood that men cannot touch their garments. The people did not respect the persons of the priests or favor the elders.

l: children and infants (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The nursing child's tongue clings to the roof of his mouth for thirst, and the young children ask for bread but no one breaks it for them. Pitiful women boiled their own children, who became their food in the destruction.

l: adversary and enemy (of Jerusalem), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The adversary and enemy entered the gates of Jerusalem, which the kings of the earth and the world's inhabitants did not believe could happen. Their pursuers were swifter than eagles, chased the people on the mountains, ambushed them in the wilderness, and hunted their steps so that they could not go in the streets.

l: famine, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: Hunger is portrayed as worse than the sword: those killed by the sword are better off than those who pine away for lack of the fruits of the field. Its effects include thirsty infants, children without bread, delicately raised people in desolation, withered skin, and mothers boiling their children.

l: destruction of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 4
s: The destruction is shown through gold dimmed, sanctuary stones poured out at every street corner, and a fire that devoured Zion's foundations. It is attributed to the LORD's wrath and the sins of the prophets and priests. The people say their end is near and their days fulfilled.

l: The Lamentations of Jeremiah, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: In this chapter, a community addresses the LORD in a prayer of lament, asking him to remember their reproach. They describe losing their inheritance to strangers, being orphaned, paying for water and wood, being pursued, and turning to Egypt and Assyria for bread. They say their fathers sinned and they bear the consequences, while servants rule them, women and young men are abused, princes and elders are dishonored, and joy has turned to mourning. They confess their own sin and grieve over the desolate mountain of Zion where foxes walk. They affirm that the LORD reigns forever, then plead for restoration while ending with the fear that he has utterly rejected them and is very angry.

l: LORD, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD is asked to remember, look at, and see the community's reproach, and is described as remaining forever with a throne from generation to generation. The speakers ask why he forgets and forsakes them, beg him to turn them to himself and renew their days, and end by saying he has utterly rejected them and is very angry against them.
